title: The Jet Engine Roars
summary: Two young inventors, one in Britain and one in Germany, each dreamed up an engine with no propeller that sucks in air, burns fuel in it and blasts it out of the back. Their jet engines made planes fly almost twice as fast. The first jet airliner had a scary problem with cracking metal, but solving it made flying much safer for everyone.

sections.heading: The Propeller Hits a Speed Limit
paragraphs: By the late 1930s, sleek metal fighters could dive at more than 700 km/h, and airliners like the DC-3 were carrying passengers across whole continents. But engineers had noticed a problem that extra horsepower could not fix. A propeller is a set of spinning wings, and its tips travel in a big circle as well as moving forward, so they go much faster than the plane. On a fast fighter the tips came close to the speed of sound, where little shock waves form and the blades waste energy shoving air about instead of pulling. Meanwhile the piston engines were turning into heavy, shaking monsters with dozens of cylinders. And high up, where thin air would let a plane fly faster on less fuel, both the engine and the propeller struggled for air.

The answer was a completely different kind of engine, with no pistons and, in its pure form, no propeller. It would suck in huge amounts of air, squeeze it, burn fuel in it and blast it out of the back. And it was invented twice, at almost the same time, by two young men in two countries who did not know each other: Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany.

Frank Whittle was born on 1 June 1907 in Coventry, an industrial city in the middle of England, where his father ran a small engineering business. In January 1923 he tried to join the Royal Air Force as an apprentice but failed the medical, partly because he was very short and slight. Whittle refused to give up. He built himself up with exercise and a better diet, applied again, and in September 1923 became an apprentice at RAF Cranwell in Lincolnshire, learning to be an aircraft mechanic.

He was so clever that in 1926 he was picked for officer training at the RAF College, Cranwell, where he also learned to fly. Cadets had to write a thesis, a long scientific essay. Whittle argued that future planes would fly very fast at great heights, where the air is thin, and would need a new kind of power. Over the next two years he realised that a gas turbine could do the whole job by itself: instead of using it to turn a propeller, he could use the hot, fast gas rushing out of the back to push the plane directly. That is a turbojet. In January 1930, aged only 22, he filed a patent for it. (A patent is an official document saying you invented something and giving you the right to control who makes it.) The patent was granted in 1932.

sections.heading: No Money, No Interest and a £5 Bill He Could Not Pay
paragraphs: You might expect the Royal Air Force to have been thrilled. It was not. Experts at the Air Ministry, the government department in charge of military flying, decided the idea was impractical. To be fair, it was a huge challenge. A jet needs a compressor that squeezes air very efficiently, and a turbine that keeps spinning at enormous speed while being blasted by gas hot enough to make ordinary metal glow and weaken. In 1930 nobody had built parts that could do that. The patent was not kept secret, so Whittle's design was published for anyone in the world to read.

For years Whittle could do very little. He was a serving officer with ordinary duties and no money to build an engine. In January 1935 his patent came up for renewal. The fee was just £5, but Whittle could not afford it and the Air Ministry would not pay, so the patent lapsed. The man who invented the jet engine could not pay a five-pound bill.

Luck turned later that year. Two former RAF officers, Rolf Dudley-Williams and James Collingwood Tinling, helped him find investors, and in March 1936 a little company called Power Jets Ltd was formed to build his engine. The RAF let Whittle work on it part-time while he studied engineering at Cambridge University. The engine was built by the British Thomson-Houston company in Rugby, which made steam turbines for power stations, and on 12 April 1937 the first Whittle engine, called the WU (Whittle Unit), was started on a test stand there. According to Whittle's own later account, the early runs were frightening: at first the engine sometimes kept speeding up even after he turned the fuel down, because fuel had pooled where it should not have, and some onlookers ran for cover. By April 1938 a rebuilt version ran for about an hour and three-quarters at 13,000 revolutions per minute. In 1938 testing moved to an empty foundry at Ladywood near Lutterworth in Leicestershire.

Short of money, Whittle rebuilt the engine again and again, often with repaired parts. Only after the Second World War began in September 1939 did the government order an engine that could fly. That engine, the W.1, first ran in April 1941. But by then Britain had already been beaten into the air by a jet built in Germany.

sections.heading: Hans von Ohain and the First Jet Flight
paragraphs: In the university town of Göttingen in Germany, a young physics student named Hans Joachim Pabst von Ohain was thinking along very similar lines. He was born in 1911, four years after Whittle. A story often told about him says he became fed up with the noise and shaking of piston-engined planes after a ride in one, and wondered whether a smooth, continuous flow of burning gas could do the job better. Whatever sparked it, by the time he finished his doctorate in physics at the University of Göttingen in 1935, he was sketching a turbojet of his own.

Von Ohain did not have money either, so he paid a car mechanic named Max Hahn, who worked at a local garage, to build a first model of his engine. It did not work well, but it was enough to show the idea was serious. In 1936 he filed a patent, and his professor introduced him to Ernst Heinkel, the owner of a big aircraft company who loved fast, record-breaking machines. Heinkel hired both von Ohain and Hahn and gave them space, money and skilled workers. This was a huge advantage that Whittle never had.

While preparing his patent, von Ohain read a copy of Whittle's published one and adjusted his own application so the two would not overlap. Historians agree that the two men reached the turbojet independently: they had the same basic idea at about the same time, the way Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz both invented calculus, and neither copied the other.

Von Ohain's team moved fast. In 1937 they ran a test engine called the HeS 1, which burned hydrogen gas because hydrogen is easy to light and burns cleanly, letting them test the compressor and turbine without fighting fuel problems. Then they built an engine that burned liquid fuel, the HeS 3, which produced roughly 4.4 kilonewtons of thrust, about the push you would need to hold up a 450-kilogram weight. It was fitted into a small, shoulder-winged test plane called the Heinkel He 178.

On 27 August 1939, at Heinkel's factory airfield at Marienehe, near the port city of Rostock on Germany's Baltic coast, test pilot Erich Warsitz opened the throttle. The He 178 rolled down the runway with a strange, rising howl and lifted into the sky. The flight lasted about six minutes. It was the first flight of an airplane powered by a turbojet engine, and it took place just five days before Germany invaded Poland and the Second World War began in Europe.

Oddly, Germany's leaders were not very impressed at first. When Heinkel showed the He 178 to senior air force officials on 1 November 1939, they reportedly thought it looked slow and unready, and the plane was never developed into a fighter. It ended up in an aviation museum in Berlin, where it was destroyed by bombing in 1943.

Decades later, Whittle and von Ohain met in person for the first time, in 1966, and again in 1978 at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, where von Ohain worked after moving to the United States in 1947. They became friendly, and in 1991 they shared the Charles Stark Draper Prize, one of the biggest awards in engineering, as co-inventors of the jet engine. That is the fairest way to remember them: two inventors, one idea, reached separately.

sections.heading: Suck, Squeeze, Bang, Blow
paragraphs: So how does a jet engine actually work? Mechanics and pilots often sum it up in four words: suck, squeeze, bang, blow. Picture a long metal tube, open at both ends, with a shaft running down the middle like the stick through a kebab.
Suck. At the front is the intake, where air rushes in. As the plane moves, air is rammed into the opening, and the spinning compressor blades just behind it grab even more.

Squeeze. The compressor is a set of fan-like blades on the spinning shaft. Whittle and von Ohain both used a centrifugal compressor, a spinning disc that flings air outward, a bit like a salad spinner throws off water. Later engines mostly use an axial compressor, rows and rows of small blades, each row squeezing the air a little more as it travels backwards. By the time the air leaves a modern compressor, it may be squashed to dozens of times its normal pressure, and it is already hot simply from being squeezed. (You can feel the same effect when you pump up a bicycle tyre and the pump gets warm.)

Bang. The squeezed air flows into the combustion chamber, where fuel, usually kerosene, is sprayed in as a fine mist and burned. It is not really a series of bangs like in a car engine. Once lit, the flame burns steadily, like a giant blowtorch. The burning makes the gas much hotter, and hot gas wants to expand, so it rushes towards the only way out: backwards.

Blow. On its way out, the hot gas rushes through the turbine, another set of blades fixed to the same shaft as the compressor. The gas spins the turbine like wind spinning a windmill, and the turbine turns the shaft, which drives the compressor at the front. This is the clever loop at the heart of the engine: the engine uses some of its own exhaust to keep sucking and squeezing fresh air. After the turbine, the gas still has plenty of energy left, and it shoots out of the nozzle at the back at very high speed.

Why does blowing gas backwards push the plane forwards? This is Newton's third law again, the same rule you met when learning how a wing turns air downwards: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The engine throws a huge mass of air backwards every second, and the air pushes the engine forwards with the same force. Think of a skateboarder throwing a heavy ball backwards and rolling forward, or a balloon zooming around a room when you let go of the neck. A jet does not push against the air behind it. It pushes on the gas it is throwing out.

The hardest part for the early inventors was the turbine. It spins thousands of times a minute while sitting in a stream of gas at many hundreds of degrees Celsius. Much of jet history since the 1930s is really the story of better metals and cooling: today's turbine blades are grown as single crystals of special alloys, with tiny holes that let cooler air flow over their surface.

sections.heading: Turbofans: The Quiet Giants on Today's Airliners
paragraphs: The engines on a modern airliner look nothing like the skinny tubes of the 1940s. They are huge and round, with an enormous curved-bladed fan you can see spinning as the plane taxis. These are turbofans.

A turbofan is a jet engine with a big extra fan bolted to the front. The middle part, called the core, is still a turbojet: suck, squeeze, bang, blow. But the turbine also drives the giant fan, and most of the air that fan pushes never goes through the core at all. It flows around the outside of the core, inside the engine's smooth outer casing, and out of the back. This is called bypass air. Engineers describe engines by their bypass ratio. A bypass ratio of 6 means that for every kilogram of air going through the hot core, six kilograms go around it. Some of today's newest airliner engines have bypass ratios of about 11 or 12.

Why go to all this trouble? It comes back to Newton again. To make a certain amount of thrust, you can either throw a small amount of air backwards very fast, or throw a large amount of air backwards more slowly. Physics shows that the second way wastes much less energy, so it uses less fuel. A turbofan does exactly that. Depending on the design, the cool bypass air can produce somewhere between about 30 and 70 percent of the engine's total thrust, and in the biggest airliner engines the fan does most of the work.

There is a wonderful bonus: noise. Most of the roar of an old jet came from its exhaust, a narrow blast of extremely fast gas tearing into the still air behind the plane. A turbofan wraps that hot, fast jet in a thick blanket of slower, cooler bypass air, so the mixing is gentler and the noise drops a lot. Sound-absorbing linings inside the engine casing quieten it further. That is why people living near airports today hear much less noise from each plane than they would have from a 1960s jet.

Turbofans developed step by step. The British Rolls-Royce Conway, which went into service around 1960, is often called the first production turbofan, though only a small amount of its air bypassed the core. The big leap came in the late 1960s with high-bypass engines like the General Electric TF39, built for a giant military cargo plane, and the Pratt & Whitney JT9D, which powered the first Boeing 747 jumbo jets. Every large airliner built today uses turbofans. Smaller planes on short routes often use turboprops instead, where a jet core turns an ordinary propeller, because at lower speeds a propeller is the most efficient way of moving lots of air.

sections.heading: The First Jets Go to War
paragraphs: Britain's first jet plane was a small, tidy aircraft built by the Gloster company, with the dull official name E.28/39. On the evening of 15 May 1941, at RAF Cranwell, the same base where Whittle had trained as a cadet, Gloster's chief test pilot Gerry Sayer climbed in, opened up the W.1 engine and took off. He flew for about 17 minutes. Whittle watched from the ground as the plane he had dreamed of for eleven years climbed away with no propeller at all, just a whistling roar. In later tests, fitted with a more powerful engine, the little plane reached more than 800 km/h. That very aircraft hangs today in the Science Museum in London.

By then the world was at war, and both sides raced to turn jets into fighters. In Germany, the Messerschmitt company designed the Me 262, a twin-engined plane with slightly swept-back wings. It first flew on jet power alone on 18 July 1942, using two Junkers Jumo 004 engines. These used the axial compressor design that most later engines followed. The Me 262 entered service in 1944 and was the world's first operational jet fighter, able to fly at more than 850 km/h, around 150 km/h faster than any Allied fighter in Europe.

It sounds like a war-winning machine, but it was not. About 1,400 were built, yet fewer than 100 were usually ready to fly at any one time. Germany was short of the special metals, like nickel and cobalt, needed for heat-resistant turbines, so the Jumo engines wore out quickly and needed a major overhaul after only about 25 hours of running. Fuel was scarce, and the jets were very vulnerable when they were slowly taking off and landing. The Me 262 arrived too late and in too small numbers to change the outcome of the war.

Britain's answer was the Gloster Meteor, powered by two Rolls-Royce Welland engines developed from Whittle's designs. It first flew on 5 March 1943, and in July 1944 No. 616 Squadron of the Royal Air Force received the first Meteors, the only Allied jet fighter to see combat in the Second World War. Their first job was to chase down V-1 flying bombs, pilotless weapons launched towards London, and the first two V-1s were brought down by Meteors on 4 August 1944. In the United States, General Electric built Whittle-type engines from British drawings, and the first American jet, the Bell XP-59 Airacomet, flew in October 1942.

The money poured into jets came from the grim needs of war, but the knowledge stayed when the fighting stopped in 1945. In November 1945 a Meteor set a world speed record of about 975 km/h, and engineers everywhere began to ask a peaceful question: if a jet could carry one pilot that fast, could it carry passengers too?

sections.heading: The Comet: Britain's Beautiful, Doomed Pioneer
paragraphs: The first country to build a jet airliner was Britain. The de Havilland company designed the Comet, a gleaming silver plane with four jet engines tucked neatly inside the roots of its wings. It first flew on 27 July 1949, piloted by John Cunningham. It looked like the future, and in many ways it was.

On 2 May 1952, the British airline BOAC began the world's first scheduled jet airliner service with paying passengers, from London to Johannesburg in South Africa, with several stops along the way to refuel. Passengers were amazed. The Comet cruised at about 750 to 800 km/h, nearly twice as fast as most propeller airliners. Because it flew high, often above 10,000 metres, it soared over much of the bad weather that tossed older planes about. With no pistons hammering away, the cabin was smooth and surprisingly quiet. It carried only around 36 to 44 passengers, but for a short while it was the most glamorous way to travel on Earth.

Then came tragedy. On 10 January 1954, a BOAC Comet broke apart in the air about 20 minutes after leaving Rome and fell into the Mediterranean Sea near the island of Elba. All 35 people on board died. The fleet was checked, small changes were made, and flights restarted. Then, on 8 April 1954, a Comet flown for South African Airways broke apart near Naples. All 21 people on board died. Every Comet was grounded, and the investigators were given an urgent mystery to solve.

To understand what went wrong, remember the pressurised cabin: sealed and pumped full of air so people can breathe high up. That makes the cabin like a balloon, blown up every time the plane climbs and let down every time it lands. The Comet flew higher than earlier airliners, so the push on its skin was bigger.

The Royal Navy helped drag wreckage from the seabed near Elba, and engineers at the Royal Aircraft Establishment in Farnborough came up with a brilliant test. They took a complete Comet fuselage and built a giant water tank around it. Then they pumped water into the cabin and let it out again, over and over, to copy the stress of real flights, while moving the wings up and down with hydraulic jacks to imitate the bumps of flying. Using water instead of air was safer: if the cabin split, water would just leak out, instead of the whole thing bursting like an exploding balloon.

On 24 June 1954, after the equivalent of 3,057 flights (1,221 real ones before the test plus 1,836 in the tank), the fuselage split open. The crack had started at the corner of an opening in the cabin's skin. In the wreckage of the Elba crash, investigators traced the break to a small cut-out in the roof, a window for a radio direction-finding aerial, where a crack had grown from a rivet hole near its corner.

This kind of failure is called metal fatigue. If you bend a paper clip back and forth, it does not break the first time, but after many bends it snaps. Each bend causes tiny damage that adds up. In the Comet, the metal around the corners of cut-outs was being stressed much more strongly than the designers had calculated, and with each pressurisation a microscopic crack crept a little further, until one day it suddenly ripped open. You may have heard that the Comet crashed because it had square windows. That is too simple. Its passenger windows actually had rounded corners. The real problem was that the skin was too thin and the stress around the corners of openings and rivet holes was far higher than expected.

The Comet's disaster taught the whole aviation world lessons that still protect you every time you fly. Later airliners were given thicker skins, rounder openings and stronger frames. They were designed to be 'fail-safe', so that if one part cracks, the load is carried by others and the crack stops before it becomes dangerous. Full-scale fatigue testing of fuselages became normal, and planes began to be inspected for tiny cracks throughout their lives. The investigation also invented new ways of rebuilding wreckage to find the cause of an accident. A redesigned Comet 4 returned to service and, on 4 October 1958, BOAC began the first regular jet passenger service across the Atlantic, between London and New York. But by then, an American rival was ready.

sections.heading: The Boeing 707 and the True Jet Age
paragraphs: In Seattle, Boeing, which built big jet bombers for the US Air Force, gambled much of its own money on a prototype jet transport, the Boeing 367-80 or 'Dash 80', which first flew on 15 July 1954. On 7 August 1955, test pilot Tex Johnston flew it over a boat race on Lake Washington in front of a huge crowd and rolled the big plane all the way over in a barrel roll. Boeing's president reportedly told him never to do it again, but it showed how strong the airplane was.

The Dash 80 became two famous aircraft: the KC-135 air-refuelling tanker for the Air Force and the Boeing 707 airliner. On 13 October 1955, Pan American World Airways, then America's leading international airline, ordered 20 Boeing 707s along with 25 of a rival jet, the Douglas DC-8. The 707 had wings swept back at a sharp angle and its four engines hung in pods under the wings, where they were easier to service and further from the cabin if something went wrong.

On 26 October 1958, a Pan Am 707 took off from New York's Idlewild Airport (now JFK) for Paris, stopping for fuel at Gander in Newfoundland. The 707 could carry well over 100 passengers, often around 140 to 180 depending on the seating, at roughly 900 km/h. That meant one jet could do the work of several propeller airliners, so tickets could slowly become cheaper. Including a close cousin called the 720, 1,010 were built, and the Douglas DC-8 soon joined it on routes all over the world.

Crossing the Atlantic now took hours instead of a long day, and people began to talk about the glamorous 'jet set'. Within a few years most big airlines were swapping their propeller fleets for jets. From Whittle's unpaid £5 bill to jets flying around the planet had taken less than 25 years.

Yet even as jets became normal, test pilots knew there was a frontier still out there. Back in the war years, pilots of the fastest propeller fighters had sometimes put their planes into steep dives and felt something terrifying. As the needle on the airspeed indicator crept higher, the whole plane began to shudder and buck. The controls went stiff or stopped working. Some planes would not come out of the dive at all. It was as if the sky itself was building an invisible wall in front of them. What was this wall, and could anyone fly through it?

deepDive: Who invented the jet engine? Historians give a split answer, and it is a good example of how invention really works. Frank Whittle filed his British patent in January 1930 and ran the first turbojet on a test stand on 12 April 1937. Hans von Ohain filed his German patent in 1936 and, with Ernst Heinkel's money behind him, got the first jet-powered aircraft, the He 178, into the air on 27 August 1939, almost two years before Britain's Gloster E.28/39 flew on 15 May 1941. So Whittle was first on paper and first to run a working engine, while von Ohain was first to fly. Other names matter too: the French engineer Maxime Guillaume patented a gas-turbine propulsion idea in 1921, A. A. Griffith in Britain worked on axial compressors, and Anselm Franz at Junkers designed the Jumo 004, the first jet engine to be mass-produced. The physics of why turbofans won is neat. Thrust equals the mass of air moved each second multiplied by how much its speed is increased. But the energy wasted in the exhaust rises with the square of the exhaust speed. So pushing a large mass of air gently (a high-bypass turbofan) gives the same thrust for much less fuel than pushing a small mass violently (a pure turbojet), which is why modern engines have bypass ratios of around 10 or more and fans over 3 metres across. Pure turbojets survived only where speed mattered more than economy, such as on Concorde. The Comet investigation is a landmark in engineering safety. The Farnborough water-tank test failed at 3,057 pressure cycles, while the two crashed aircraft had made about 1,290 and 900 pressurised flights. The Cohen inquiry found that stresses around cut-outs were far higher than de Havilland had calculated. Engineers argue about how much blame to put on construction details such as countersunk rivet holes, but all agree on the main lesson: structures that are loaded again and again must be designed and tested for fatigue, not just for a single big load. 'Fail-safe' and later 'damage-tolerant' design, now required by aviation regulators around the world, grew directly out of the Comet disasters.
funFact: In 1935 Frank Whittle let his jet engine patent lapse because he could not afford the £5 renewal fee.
